title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
oneLiner: Passes a request along a chain of handlers, each deciding to handle it or hand it off, until someone actually does.

hero.name: The Relay
hero.catchphrase: Not my job? Pass it on. Someone in this chain will catch it.
hero.power: Passes a request down a chain of handlers, each free to handle it, transform it, or hand it to the next link.
hero.weakness: If nobody in the chain claims the request, it can silently vanish at the end with no error — a chain needs a fallback handler or it can fail quietly.
hero.origin: The Relay appeared inside a support-ticket router with a single 200-line function deciding whether a ticket should go to tier 1, tier 2, billing, or engineering, all in one giant if/else.

story.problem: `routeTicket()` is one 200-line function full of nested if/else, deciding whether a support ticket goes to tier 1, tier 2, billing, or engineering. Every new routing rule means editing this one fragile function.
story.solution: The Relay turns each routing rule into its own `Handler` in a chain. Each handler checks if it can handle the ticket; if not, it passes it to the next handler in line.
story.result: Tickets flow through the chain until a handler claims them. Adding a new routing rule means inserting one new handler — the rest of the chain doesn't change.

before: One giant function decides every routing rule
Adding a rule means editing shared, fragile logic
Routing order is buried inside nested conditionals
after: Each routing rule is an independent handler in a chain
Adding a rule means inserting one new handler
Routing order is explicit — the order handlers are chained in

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: routeTicket() is a 200-line wall of nested if/else, checking every routing rule in one place.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We need a new rule for VIP customers. That means adding another branch to this already-unreadable function.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Relay lines up four handlers, each ready to catch the ticket or pass it down the line.
panels.speaker: The Relay
panels.dialogue: Stop cramming every rule into one function. Line up your handlers instead — each one decides for itself: handle it, or pass it on.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Tier1Handler checks the ticket first. If it can't handle it, it calls next.handle(ticket) — passing to BillingHandler, then EngineeringHandler.
panels.speaker: The Relay
panels.dialogue: Each handler only knows its own rule. If it's not the right one, it passes the ticket along — no handler needs to know about the others.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: VipHandler ships as one new link at the front of the chain. The other handlers are untouched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One new handler, inserted at the front of the chain. Nothing else in the routing logic had to change.

useWhen: A request needs to be handled by one of several possible handlers, but which one isn't known until runtime.
You want to add or reorder handling rules without touching a monolithic routing function.
Each handler's decision logic is independent and shouldn't need to know about the other handlers.
avoidWhen: There's a small, fixed number of routing rules that never change — a simple if/else is easier to read at a glance.
Every request must be handled by ALL handlers in sequence (that's closer to a pipeline/middleware pattern, not chain-of-responsibility's 'stop at first match').
You need a guarantee that a request is always handled — chains without a fallback can silently drop requests.
commonMistakes: Building a chain with no fallback/default handler, so an unmatched request silently disappears at the end.
Letting handlers depend on each other's internals instead of just deciding independently whether to handle or pass along.
Making the chain order implicit or hard to discover, so nobody can predict which handler will actually catch a given request.
Confusing Chain of Responsibility (one handler claims the request) with a middleware pipeline (every layer runs, in sequence).
explanation.realWorldExample: HTTP middleware pipelines (each middleware can handle, modify, or pass the request along), event bubbling in the DOM (a click event travels up through ancestor handlers), and support-ticket or approval-request routing systems are all Chain of Responsibility (or close cousins of it).

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just a fancy if/else chain?

conversation.speaker: The Relay
conversation.message: The outcome looks similar, but the shape is different. Each handler doesn't know about the others — it just decides 'can I handle this?' and passes along if not. You can reorder or insert handlers without touching the others' code at all.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What happens if nothing in the chain handles the request?

conversation.speaker: The Relay
conversation.message: That's my real weakness — silence. Always end your chain with a fallback handler, or you'll have requests vanishing with no error and no trace.

codeBattle.scenario: Your expense-approval system routes requests: managers approve under $500, directors approve under $5,000, and the CFO approves anything above that — and finance keeps adding new approval tiers.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Relay lets each approval tier be its own handler that either approves the request or passes it up the chain, so adding a new tier means inserting one new link.

quiz.question: What is the core behavior of Chain of Responsibility?
options: A request passes through a chain of handlers until one of them handles it
Every handler in the chain always processes the request in sequence
A single handler processes all possible request types
Requests are queued and processed in a random order
quiz.answer: A request passes through a chain of handlers until one of them handles it
quiz.explanation: The chain stops (typically) once a handler claims the request — that's the defining shape of the pattern.

quiz.question: What is a common bug risk with Chain of Responsibility?
options: A request reaches the end of the chain unhandled and silently disappears
Every handler always processes every request, causing duplication
Handlers must know about every other handler in the chain
The chain can only ever have one handler
quiz.answer: A request reaches the end of the chain unhandled and silently disappears
quiz.explanation: Without a fallback handler, an unmatched request can vanish with no error, making bugs hard to trace.

quiz.question: What benefit does Chain of Responsibility provide over one large if/else function?
options: New handling rules can be added or reordered without touching existing handlers' code
It runs strictly faster in every case
It removes the need for any conditional logic
quiz.answer: New handling rules can be added or reordered without touching existing handlers' code
quiz.explanation: Each handler is independent, so extending or reordering the chain doesn't require editing existing logic.

quiz.question: How does Chain of Responsibility differ from a middleware pipeline where every layer always runs?
options: Chain of Responsibility typically stops at the first handler that claims the request; a pipeline runs every layer regardless
They are exactly the same pattern
Middleware pipelines can only have one layer
Chain of Responsibility requires a database
quiz.answer: Chain of Responsibility typically stops at the first handler that claims the request; a pipeline runs every layer regardless
quiz.explanation: The 'stop at first match' behavior is what distinguishes classic Chain of Responsibility from a full middleware pipeline.
